question: Which type of pathogen causes malaria?
options: Bacterium
Virus
Fungus
Protist

question: How do bacteria cause disease in the body?
options: By invading host cells and replicating inside them
By releasing toxins into the body
By blocking blood vessels
By destroying antibodies
correct: By releasing toxins into the body

question: How is HIV transmitted?
options: Through contaminated food and water
Through the bite of a mosquito
Through sexual contact or exchange of blood
Through droplets in the air
correct: Through sexual contact or exchange of blood

question: What effect does Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) have on plants?
options: It causes black spots on leaves
It causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration reducing photosynthesis
It causes the plant's roots to rot
It blocks the xylem preventing water transport
correct: It causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration reducing photosynthesis

question: What is the role of cilia in the trachea?
options: To produce mucus to trap pathogens
To beat and move mucus and trapped pathogens away from the lungs
To kill bacteria using hydrochloric acid
To produce antibodies against pathogens
correct: To beat and move mucus and trapped pathogens away from the lungs

question: What do lymphocytes produce in response to an infection?
options: Antigens
Antibodies
Toxins
Enzymes

question: What is the role of memory cells?
options: To engulf and digest pathogens directly
To produce toxins that kill pathogens
To remain after infection and allow a faster response if the same pathogen returns
To carry oxygen around the body
correct: To remain after infection and allow a faster response if the same pathogen returns

question: How do vaccines work?
options: They kill all bacteria in the body
They introduce a dead or weakened pathogen to stimulate an immune response
They replace white blood cells with stronger ones
They block viruses from entering cells
correct: They introduce a dead or weakened pathogen to stimulate an immune response

question: Why do antibiotics not work against viral infections?
options: Viruses are too small for antibiotics to find
Antibiotics only target processes found in bacterial cells, not viruses
Viruses produce antibodies that destroy the antibiotics
Antibiotics are only effective in the stomach
correct: Antibiotics only target processes found in bacterial cells, not viruses

question: What is a placebo used for in a clinical trial?
options: To give all patients the new drug
To act as a control so results can be compared to the real treatment
To test the drug on animals first
To speed up the drug testing process
correct: To act as a control so results can be compared to the real treatment

question: How is Salmonella spread?
options: Through sexual contact
Through the bite of a mosquito
Through contaminated food
Through droplets in the air

question: Which organism transmits malaria to humans?
options: A tick
The Anopheles mosquito
A rat
A housefly

question: What is a double blind trial?
options: A trial where only doctors know who receives the drug
A trial where neither patients nor doctors know who receives the real drug or placebo
A trial where all patients receive the real drug
A trial where the drug is tested on two different diseases
correct: A trial where neither patients nor doctors know who receives the real drug or placebo

question: Which of the following is a concern about antibiotic resistance?
options: Antibiotics will start working against viruses
Resistant bacteria will evolve and spread, making infections harder to treat
Patients will become immune to all diseases
Antibiotics will become too expensive to produce
correct: Resistant bacteria will evolve and spread, making infections harder to treat

question: What is phagocytosis?
options: The production of antibodies by lymphocytes
The process by which phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens
The release of toxins by bacteria
The movement of white blood cells through blood vessel walls
correct: The process by which phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens

question: A microorganism that causes disease is called a __________.
White blood cells called __________ engulf and destroy pathogens.
Proteins produced by lymphocytes that bind to specific antigens are called __________.
When enough people are vaccinated to prevent the spread of disease, this is called __________ immunity.
Drugs that kill bacteria but do not work against viruses are called __________.
The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by __________.
Malaria is caused by a __________ and transmitted by mosquitoes.
The stomach produces __________ to kill pathogens in food and drink.
A unique protein on the surface of a pathogen that triggers an immune response is called an __________.
HIV eventually leads to __________, where the immune system can no longer fight infections.
Match each disease to its type of pathogen.
Match each defence to how it protects the body.

pairs.definition: Acts as a physical barrier preventing pathogens from entering
Traps pathogens in the nose and trachea
Beat to move mucus and trapped pathogens away from the lungs

question: Match each immune system term to its correct description.

pairs.definition: White blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens
White blood cell that produces antibodies
Protein that binds specifically to an antigen on a pathogen
Long-lived cell that allows a faster response to the same pathogen

question: Match each drug type to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Kills or inhibits bacteria but not viruses
Inhibits the development of viruses inside host cells
Relieves symptoms such as pain but does not kill the pathogen

question: Match each viral disease to how it is transmitted.

pairs.definition: Spread by droplets from sneezes and coughs
Spread through sexual contact or exchange of blood

question: State what is meant by the term pathogen.
mark_scheme: A microorganism that causes disease (1).

question: State why antibiotics cannot be used to treat viral infections.
mark_scheme: Antibiotics only target processes in bacterial cells (1); viruses replicate inside host cells using the host's own machinery (1) — accept either point.

question: Name the scientist who discovered penicillin.
mark_scheme: Alexander Fleming (1).

question: State what is meant by herd immunity.
mark_scheme: When enough people in a population are vaccinated that pathogens cannot spread easily (1); protecting unvaccinated individuals (1) — accept either point.

question: Explain how phagocytes defend the body against infection.
mark_scheme: Phagocytes detect and move towards pathogens (1); engulf the pathogen (1); enzymes digest and destroy the pathogen (1) — any two.

question: Explain how a vaccine protects a person against future infection.
mark_scheme: Vaccine introduces dead or weakened pathogen / antigens (1); white blood cells produce antibodies (1); memory cells are produced (1); if the real pathogen enters, a faster and larger immune response occurs (1) — any two.

question: Describe two ways in which pathogens can be spread between people.
mark_scheme: Through the air / droplets from sneezing or coughing (1); direct contact / touching (1); contaminated food or water (1); through a vector e.g. mosquito (1); exchange of body fluids (1) — any two.

question: Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in bacteria.
mark_scheme: Random mutation produces resistant bacteria (1); antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria (1); resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (1); resistance genes passed to offspring (1) — any two.

question: Describe what happens during a double blind clinical trial.
mark_scheme: Some patients receive the real drug, others receive a placebo (1); neither the patients nor the doctors know who receives which (1); reduces bias in the results (1) — any two.

question: Explain how the immune system responds to a pathogen it has not encountered before.
mark_scheme: Pathogen has antigens on its surface (1); lymphocytes detect the antigens (1); lymphocytes produce specific antibodies (1); antibodies bind to antigens and destroy the pathogen (1); memory cells are produced (1) — any three.

question: Explain the difference between how viruses and bacteria cause disease.
mark_scheme: Bacteria are living cells that release toxins (1); toxins damage tissues and cause symptoms (1); viruses are not living / not cells (1); viruses invade host cells and replicate inside them (1); this damages or destroys the host cells (1) — any three.

question: Describe the stages involved in testing a new drug before it can be prescribed to patients.
mark_scheme: Pre-clinical testing on cells / tissues / animals (1); checks for toxicity / efficacy / dosage (1); clinical trials on human volunteers (1); tested against a placebo (1); double blind trial used to prevent bias (1); approved by regulatory bodies (1) — any three.

question: Explain how vaccination protects both individuals and populations from infectious disease.
mark_scheme: Vaccine contains dead or weakened pathogen / antigens (1); immune system produces antibodies (1); memory cells remain (1); faster response if pathogen encountered again (1); herd immunity — if enough people vaccinated pathogen cannot spread (1); protects those who cannot be vaccinated e.g. babies / immunocompromised (1) — any four.

question: Describe the non-specific and specific defences the human body uses to fight infection.
mark_scheme: Non-specific: skin as physical barrier (1); mucus traps pathogens (1); cilia move mucus (1); stomach acid kills pathogens (1). Specific: phagocytes engulf pathogens (1); lymphocytes produce specific antibodies (1); memory cells for future immunity (1) — any four.

question: Explain why antibiotic resistance is a serious global health concern and describe steps that can be taken to reduce it.
mark_scheme: Resistant bacteria cannot be killed by current antibiotics (1); infections become harder to treat (1); resistance spreads through populations (1); steps: only prescribe when necessary (1); complete full course of antibiotics (1); develop new antibiotics (1) — any four.

question: Explain how malaria is transmitted and describe methods used to control its spread.
mark_scheme: Malaria caused by a protist (1); transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito — a vector (1); mosquito bites infected person then bites healthy person (1); control methods: insecticides to kill mosquitoes (1); mosquito nets to prevent bites (1); draining stagnant water where mosquitoes breed (1); antiviral drugs (1) — any four.

question: Explain the difference between the primary and secondary immune response. Why does a secondary infection with the same pathogen result in milder or no symptoms?
mark_scheme: Primary response: first encounter with pathogen (1); takes time to produce enough antibodies (1); symptoms develop during this time (1). Secondary response: memory cells recognise the antigen (1); faster and larger antibody production (1); pathogen destroyed before symptoms develop (1); explains basis of vaccination (1) — any five.

question: Evaluate the use of vaccination programmes to control infectious diseases. Include arguments for and against vaccination in your answer.
mark_scheme: For: prevents disease in vaccinated individuals (1); herd immunity protects whole population (1); has eradicated diseases e.g. smallpox (1); cost-effective compared to treating disease (1). Against: some people have side effects (1); some people object on religious or ethical grounds (1); vaccines may not be 100% effective (1); some pathogens mutate so vaccines become less effective (1) — any six points.

question: Explain the process of developing a new drug from discovery to being available to patients. Include why this process takes a long time.
mark_scheme: Discovery of potential drug compound (1); pre-clinical testing on cells and animals (1); checks for toxicity / side effects / efficacy (1); clinical trials on human volunteers (1); placebo used as control (1); double blind trial to avoid bias (1); tested on larger groups over time (1); regulatory approval required (1); process takes years to ensure safety (1) — any six.

question: Explain the difference between bacteria, viruses and fungi as pathogens. Include one disease caused by each type.
mark_scheme: Bacteria: single-celled prokaryotes that reproduce rapidly and release toxins, e.g. Salmonella (1); viruses: non-living particles that invade cells and replicate inside them, e.g. influenza (1); fungi: eukaryotic organisms that can infect skin/organs, e.g. athlete's foot (1); each type requires a different treatment — bacteria: antibiotics; viruses: antivirals/vaccines (1).

question: Describe how the HIV virus causes AIDS. Include how HIV is transmitted and why AIDS is life-threatening.
mark_scheme: HIV attacks white blood cells / T-helper lymphocytes (1); reduces the number of immune cells available (1); AIDS occurs when immune system is so weakened it cannot fight infections (1); person becomes susceptible to 'opportunistic infections' that a healthy immune system would easily overcome (1).

question: Explain how Salmonella bacteria cause food poisoning. Include how it is spread and the role of toxins.
mark_scheme: Salmonella is ingested in contaminated food / undercooked poultry (1); bacteria multiply in the gut (1); bacteria produce toxins (1); toxins cause symptoms: vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach cramps, fever (1).

question: Describe three physical or chemical barriers the human body uses to prevent pathogens from entering.
mark_scheme: Skin: forms a physical barrier, prevents entry (1); mucus in the breathing system traps pathogens (1); stomach acid (HCl) kills pathogens in food (1); cilia in the trachea sweep mucus away from lungs (1). Accept: nose hairs trap particles / tears contain lysozyme.

question: Explain what is meant by the term 'specific immune response'. Include the role of antigens and antibodies.
mark_scheme: Each pathogen has specific antigens on its surface (1); white blood cells (lymphocytes) produce antibodies specific to those antigens (1); antibodies bind to antigens — complementary shape (1); this leads to destruction of the pathogen, and memory cells remain for future infections (1).

question: Explain how malaria is transmitted and why it is difficult to control.
mark_scheme: Malaria is caused by a Plasmodium protist (1); transmitted via the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes (1); mosquito acts as a vector — carries the pathogen without being infected (1); difficult to control: mosquitoes widespread, insecticides harmful to environment, Plasmodium is developing drug resistance (1).

question: Describe how vaccination protects both an individual and a population (herd immunity).
mark_scheme: Vaccine contains dead/weakened/fragment of pathogen (1); body produces antibodies and memory cells without suffering the disease (1); if exposed later, rapid antibody production prevents illness (1); herd immunity: if enough people are vaccinated, pathogen cannot spread — protects those who cannot be vaccinated (1).

question: Explain how the measles virus spreads and describe the complications that can arise from measles infection.
mark_scheme: Measles spreads via respiratory droplets / airborne transmission (1); highly contagious — one infected person can infect ~18 others (1); complications: pneumonia, encephalitis (brain inflammation) (1); MMR vaccine provides effective protection — second dose gives ~97% immunity (1).

question: Evaluate the use of antibiotics in treating bacterial infections. Include why antibiotics do not work against viruses and the problem of antibiotic resistance.
mark_scheme: Antibiotics kill or inhibit growth of bacteria — effective against bacterial infections (1); antibiotics do not work on viruses — viruses do not have the cell structures antibiotics target (1); antibiotic resistance: random mutations produce bacteria that survive antibiotic treatment (1); resistant strains reproduce and spread — fewer effective treatments available (1).

question: Describe the precautions taken in hospitals to prevent the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA.
mark_scheme: Regular hand washing with soap and alcohol gel (1); isolation of infected patients (1); screening patients for MRSA before admission (1); cleaning surfaces with disinfectants; use of personal protective equipment (PPE) (1).

question: Explain why the secondary immune response is faster and stronger than the primary immune response.
mark_scheme: After first infection, memory cells are produced (1); memory cells remain in the bloodstream for many years (1); on second exposure to same antigen, memory cells divide rapidly (1); large quantities of antibodies produced quickly before symptoms develop (1).

question: Explain how the body responds to a bacterial infection. Include both non-specific and specific defences and the role of phagocytes and lymphocytes.
mark_scheme: Non-specific: inflammation at site of infection — increased blood flow (1); phagocytes engulf bacteria by phagocytosis (1); specific: lymphocytes detect antigens on bacteria (1); B lymphocytes produce specific antibodies (1); T lymphocytes destroy infected cells; memory cells form for future exposure (1).

question: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using vaccines to control infectious diseases at a population level.
mark_scheme: Advantages: prevents disease without risk of infection (1); creates herd immunity — protects vulnerable people who cannot be vaccinated (1); eradicated some diseases — e.g. smallpox (1); Disadvantages: some vaccines have rare side effects (1); requires high uptake in population to achieve herd immunity; some pathogens mutate rapidly requiring new vaccines (1).

question: Explain how scientists develop and test new drugs to treat infectious diseases. Include the stages from laboratory testing to clinical trials.
mark_scheme: Drug tested on cells/tissues in laboratory — checks for toxicity (1); tested on animals — checks effectiveness and safety at larger scale (1); clinical trials: drug tested on healthy volunteers at low dose first (1); then tested on patients — double-blind trials compare drug vs placebo (1); data analysed — drug only approved if safe and effective (1).

question: Describe how scientists work to control the spread of malaria. Include biological, chemical and physical methods.
mark_scheme: Insecticides: spray mosquito breeding sites with chemicals to kill larvae (1); insecticide-treated bed nets prevent mosquito biting at night (1); draining stagnant water to remove mosquito breeding sites (1); biological control: using natural predators of mosquitoes (1); antimalarial drugs reduce symptoms and prevent death (1).

question: Explain how the influenza virus causes disease and why new flu vaccines are needed each year.
mark_scheme: Influenza virus infects cells in the respiratory tract (1); replicates inside host cells and destroys them (1); causes symptoms: fever, muscle aches, fatigue (1); influenza virus mutates frequently — antigens on surface change (1); existing antibodies / memory cells no longer recognise new strain — new vaccine needed annually (1).

question: Describe how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics. Explain why this is a major global health concern.
mark_scheme: Random mutations occur in bacterial DNA (1); some mutations make bacteria less susceptible to antibiotics (1); bacteria with resistant mutation survive and reproduce (1); resistant strain passes on resistance — natural selection (1); concern: fewer effective antibiotics available; infections become untreatable; resistant strains spread globally (1).

question: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat cancer. Include how they are made and two ways they can target cancer cells.
mark_scheme: Mouse immunised with tumour antigen — produces lymphocytes (1); lymphocytes fused with myeloma cells to make hybridoma cells (1); hybridoma cells produce large quantities of identical antibodies specific to tumour antigen (1); carry radioactive isotope directly to tumour — targeted radiation therapy (1); carry chemotherapy drug directly to cancer cells — reduces side effects on healthy tissue (1).

question: Compare the way HIV and influenza viruses cause disease. Include how each is transmitted and the long-term effects on health.
mark_scheme: HIV: sexually transmitted / blood contact; influenza: respiratory droplets (1); HIV attacks T-helper lymphocytes — progressive immune destruction (1); influenza attacks respiratory epithelial cells — acute infection (1); HIV leads to AIDS if untreated — susceptibility to opportunistic infections (1); influenza usually self-limiting but can be fatal in elderly/immunocompromised (1).

question: Describe how non-specific physical and chemical defences work together to prevent pathogens from entering the body.
mark_scheme: Skin: tough barrier, produces acidic secretions that inhibit bacterial growth (1); cilia in trachea: beat to sweep mucus with trapped pathogens up to throat (1); mucus traps bacteria and viruses (1); stomach acid (pH 2) kills most bacteria in food (1); tears contain lysozyme enzyme — breaks down bacterial cell walls (1).

question: Evaluate the claim that vaccination has been the most important medical advance in human history. Include evidence for and against this claim.
mark_scheme: For: smallpox eradicated globally through vaccination (1); dramatic reduction in measles, polio, diphtheria deaths (1); herd immunity protects entire populations (1); cost-effective compared to treating illness (1); Against: improved sanitation/clean water also reduced disease (1) / no vaccine exists for many diseases e.g. HIV, malaria; antibiotic resistant bacteria increasing (1) — 5 marks for balanced discussion.

question: Explain how the immune system responds to infection and how vaccination exploits this response to provide protection. Include the roles of B-cells, T-cells, antibodies and memory cells.
mark_scheme: Pathogen enters body; non-specific response (phagocytosis) begins (1); B lymphocytes identify specific antigens on pathogen surface (1); B cells differentiate and produce specific antibodies (1); antibodies bind to antigens — pathogen neutralised or destroyed (1); T-killer cells destroy infected body cells (1); memory B and T cells remain — rapid response on re-exposure (1). Vaccination: introduces harmless antigen — stimulates same response without disease, creating memory cells (bonus for clarity — any 6 points).

question: Evaluate different methods of controlling the spread of communicable diseases at a global level. Include vaccination, antibiotics, quarantine and improved sanitation.
mark_scheme: Vaccination: prevents disease in individuals, creates herd immunity — most effective for viral diseases (1); antibiotics: treat bacterial infections but overuse leads to resistance (1); quarantine: isolating infected individuals slows spread but impractical for mild illness (1); improved sanitation / clean water: prevents spread of water-borne diseases like cholera (1); each method has limitations — vaccines take years to develop; sanitation improvements costly (1); most effective approach combines multiple strategies (1).

question: Describe the problem of antibiotic resistance and evaluate the measures that can be taken to slow its spread.
mark_scheme: Antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection — resistant bacteria survive treatment (1); resistant genes passed to offspring / can be transferred between bacteria by plasmids (1); MRSA example — resistant to most antibiotics (1); measures: only prescribe antibiotics when essential (1); complete the full course of antibiotics (1); develop new antibiotics — but expensive and slow (1). Accept: better hygiene in hospitals / surveillance of resistance patterns.

question: Explain the life cycle of the malaria parasite and why malaria is particularly difficult to treat and prevent.
mark_scheme: Plasmodium parasite transmitted by female Anopheles mosquito bite (1); parasite enters bloodstream, travels to liver and reproduces (1); then enters and destroys red blood cells in cycles — causes cyclical fever (1); treatment: anti-malarial drugs target the parasite but resistance is developing (1); prevention: insecticide-treated nets, draining standing water, mosquito repellents (1); challenge: parasite has complex life cycle in two hosts; mosquitoes widespread in tropical regions; poverty limits access to prevention measures (1).

question: Evaluate the use of monoclonal antibodies in medicine. Include how they are produced, their diagnostic uses, therapeutic uses, and any limitations.
mark_scheme: Production: immunise mouse → collect B lymphocytes → fuse with myeloma cells → hybridoma produces monoclonal antibodies (1); diagnostic: home pregnancy test detects hCG hormone (1); cancer diagnosis: labelled antibodies locate tumour cells in scans (1); therapeutic: carry chemotherapy drug specifically to cancer cells (1); advantages: highly specific, reduce side effects compared to traditional chemotherapy (1); limitations: expensive, some patients have side effects, require ongoing development (1).

question: Explain how the development of antiseptics and antibiotics has changed medicine. Include who discovered each and the impact on infection rates.
mark_scheme: Ignaz Semmelweis: showed handwashing reduced childbed fever deaths — early evidence for germ theory (1); Joseph Lister: introduced carbolic acid spray as antiseptic during surgery — reduced surgical infections (1); Alexander Fleming: discovered penicillin from Penicillium mould (1); Florey and Chain: developed penicillin for medical use in World War II (1); dramatic reduction in deaths from infection — e.g. wound infections, pneumonia (1); now threatened by antibiotic resistance — importance of careful stewardship (1).

question: The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated both the power and limitations of modern medicine. Evaluate the scientific response to the pandemic, including vaccine development, antiviral drugs, and public health measures.
mark_scheme: Vaccines developed in under a year using mRNA technology — new approach (1); trials showed >90% effectiveness at preventing severe disease (1); antivirals (e.g. antiprotease drugs) reduced hospitalisation for high-risk groups (1); public health measures: social distancing, masks, quarantine reduced transmission (1); limitations: vaccine hesitancy reduced uptake; virus mutated (variants) reducing vaccine effectiveness over time (1); global inequality: wealthy nations vaccinated faster than poorer nations (1).

question: Explain how a new drug is developed and trialled before it becomes available to patients. Include ethical considerations in clinical trials.
mark_scheme: Drug initially tested in laboratory on cells or tissues — checks basic toxicity (1); animal testing checks for safety and efficacy before human use (1); Phase I clinical trial: small group of healthy volunteers — checks safety and dosage (1); Phase II: patients given drug — checks effectiveness and side effects (1); Phase III: large-scale double-blind randomised controlled trial — compared against placebo or existing treatment (1); ethics: informed consent required; participants can withdraw; double-blind prevents bias (1).

question: Explain how scientists use double-blind trials to test new drugs. Include the roles of the control group, placebo, and why neither patients nor doctors know who receives the drug.
mark_scheme: Participants randomly assigned to treatment or control group (1); control group receives a placebo — identical in appearance but no active drug (1); double-blind: neither the patient nor the doctor knows who receives the drug (1); this prevents bias — doctors cannot unconsciously treat patients differently (1); results compared between groups to determine drug effectiveness (1).
